analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to provide paid sick time and creates a federal paid family leave insurance program.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced during the COVID-19 emergency, was referred to five House committees, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the temporary COVID-era paid leave law with a permanent program. Every worker — including independent contractors — would earn at least 1 hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year. During any declared public health emergency, workers would immediately get up to 14 additional paid sick days and 12 weeks of paid leave at two-thirds pay, and the Treasury would reimburse employers for that emergency leave. It would also create a Social Security Administration program paying up to 60 days of partial wage replacement for family and medical leave, funded by a new employer payroll tax and employee income tax.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with no paid sick leave — disproportionately low-wage, part-time, and hourly workers — would gain the first federal guarantee of earned paid sick time. Independent contractors would be covered explicitly, regardless of how their employer classifies them. Workers facing domestic violence or stalking could use sick time for medical care, relocation, or court proceedings. During public health emergencies, workers could take leave immediately with no waiting period and no doctor's note, and could not be fired or disciplined for using it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid sick leave, including contractors

how_it_helps.text: Employers must grant at least 1 hour of accrued paid sick time per 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours (7 days) a year, usable for the worker's own illness or medical care, a family member's care, workplace or school closures during a public health emergency, or domestic violence and stalking-related needs.

On the day a public health emergency is declared, every covered worker immediately gets up to 14 additional days of paid sick time, regardless of how long they have been employed, with no certification or documentation allowed during the emergency.

During a public health emergency, workers are entitled to 12 weeks of emergency paid leave at not less than two-thirds of their regular pay (or the applicable minimum wage), and the Treasury reimburses employers for those wages within days.

The bill creates a family and medical leave insurance program inside the Social Security Administration paying up to 60 days of partially-paid leave, with a maximum monthly benefit of $4,000 starting in 2022.

Coverage extends to individuals performing labor for pay regardless of whether the employer classifies them as independent contractors, and courts cannot compel workers into individual arbitration for claims under the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost of the permanent annual accrued sick time, and a new employer payroll tax (paired with an employee income tax) funds the leave insurance program. During declared public health emergencies, the federal Treasury — general taxpayers — pays employers back for emergency sick leave and leave, so the emergency provisions add to federal spending. All businesses of any size with even one employee are covered.

drawbacks.text: The permanent sick-time mandate is a genuine cost for employers, including small businesses with thin margins, and unlike emergency leave it is not reimbursed; a single-employee shop is covered the same as a large corporation.
The leave insurance program is funded by a new employer payroll tax and a new employee income tax, which would come out of wages and business costs even in years when few workers use the benefit.

Employer reimbursement is largely automatic: if the Labor Secretary does not rule on an employer's affidavit within 5 business days, the claim is deemed valid, a design that invites questionable claims even though both Secretaries may investigate and recover fraud.
The 12-week emergency paid leave provision itself sunsets on December 31, 2021, so the bill's most generous leave benefit is temporary even in the version introduced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary workers the bill is a large, concrete gain: the United States is one of the few wealthy countries with no guaranteed paid sick time, and this bill would have locked in both a permanent accrual and a standing emergency system. The costs are real — employer mandates, a new payroll tax, and federal reimbursement during emergencies — and the reimbursement design is loose enough that an honest supporter should acknowledge fraud exposure. On balance the benefits to workers outweigh the costs, though the payroll-tax funding structure and the sunset on emergency leave make it a less complete program than its title suggests.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on April 3, 2020 during the COVID-19 emergency and split among five House committees, none of which ever acted on it; it never got a hearing or a floor vote and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on April 3, 2020, weeks after the COVID-19 public health emergency was declared, with 38 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the Education and Labor, Ways and Means, Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Judiciary committees.
No committee took it up; the full action history shows nothing after the initial referral.
The bill would have repealed the temporary leave provisions of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act and replaced them with a permanent sick-time mandate and emergency leave system.
The 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 without the bill ever reaching the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed permanent paid sick time and the new payroll tax are better off, because the leave provisions of the Families First Coronavirus Response Act expired on their own schedule and no permanent federal guarantee was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that avoided the sick-time mandate

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 3, 2020 and led the effort for a permanent paid sick time and paid leave system.

for.name: 38 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record.

against.name: House leadership and five committee chairs
against.role: Speaker and the chairs of Education and Labor, Ways and Means, Oversight and Reform, House Administration, and Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action; the bill sat with the five committees from April 3, 2020 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 38 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors in the record, and the House's Democratic majority never brought it to a vote.

industries.industry: Employers of low-wage and hourly workers (retail, food service, hospitality, care work)
industries.note: These employers face the largest added cost from a guaranteed accrual of up to 56 hours of paid sick time a year for their predominantly unsick-leave-covered workforces. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the workers who would have gained the guarantee.

All employers would owe the permanent sick-time accrual and a new payroll tax, but during declared public health emergencies the Treasury reimburses them for the emergency sick leave and 12 weeks of paid leave they provide, largely covering those wage costs. That reimbursement was designed to make emergency leave affordable to even the smallest employers.

The bill explicitly covers individuals performing labor for pay regardless of independent-contractor classification, so gig workers would gain sick time their platforms do not provide, and platforms would bear a cost they currently avoid through contractor classification.
